name: Bisoctrizole
lead: Bisoctrizole (INCI: methylene bis-benzotriazolyl tetramethylbutylphenol, MBBT; trade names Tinosorb M, Parsol Max) is a phenolic bis-benzotriazole UV absorber used in sunscreens. It is made as microfine particles, usually supplied as a roughly 50% aqueous suspension, and is described as a hybrid between organic and particulate filters.[1][2] Its place in an appearance routine is as a daily UV filter: broad-spectrum sunscreen is how people try to limit the sun exposure associated with tanning, uneven pigmentation and visible photoageing.
It covers UVB and UVA and is reported to show little photodegradation. It is approved in the EU and other regions but has not been approved by the US FDA as a sunscreen active.[1][2]

Research is mostly formulation, skin-penetration and environmental work. One small registered trial examined it alongside titanium dioxide in solar urticaria; no study has examined it as an appearance treatment.

paras: Bisoctrizole dissolves poorly in both oil and water, so it is typically formulated as a particle suspension in the water phase, stabilised by a surfactant such as decyl glucoside.[2] Wikipedia says it is reported to help stabilise other filters, especially octinoxate, while flagging these claims as needing better citation.[2] A US drug label shows it combined with ethylhexyl triazone, diethylhexyl butamido triazone and DHHB in one product.[3]
Grokipedia adds that it is also used in some maxillofacial silicone prosthetics to resist UV degradation.[1]

Wikipedia gives the compound's melting point as about 196 C and lists additional names including UV-360, Eversorb M and Milestab 360, the latter names reflecting its industrial use as a plastics stabiliser.[2] The particles are under about 200 nm, and the article describes it as a hybrid that is organic in chemistry but behaves as a particulate filter.[2] The same article describes it as a broad-spectrum absorber covering UVB and UVA, though it flags some of its statements on how the particles scatter light as needing better sourcing.[2]
Because it shows very little photodegradation, formulators use it in combination with other filters; the multi-filter US label cited above pairs it with triazine and hexyl benzoate filters.[2][3]

Sun protection is among the most commonly cited ways to keep skin looking even and youthful, because ultraviolet exposure drives tanning, pigmentation and photoageing. A sunscreen filter like bisoctrizole matters to an appearance routine mainly through UVA coverage. The SPF number measures protection against sunburn-producing UVB and does not capture UVA, and conventional sunscreens have been described as blocking little UVA relative to their SPF [11]. Regulators therefore define broad-spectrum protection separately: the US definition, in effect since 2012, requires UVA protection proportional to UVB protection, the EU requires a UVA protection factor of at least one third of the SPF, Japan uses a PA rating from PA+ to PA++++, and the UK and Ireland use a star system [11].

Wikipedia's sunscreen article also notes that people typically apply only a quarter to a half of the amount used in laboratory SPF testing, so effective protection can be lower than the label figure [11]. Filters that are photostable, such as bisoctrizole, are of interest to formulators because they keep their protection through a day in the sun [2].

A comparison of UVA protection from sunscreens containing butyl methoxydibenzoylmethane, MBBT or microfine zinc oxide used in vivo and in vitro methods.[4] In vitro percutaneous absorption work compared an organic and a mineral sunscreen and measured distribution in the stratum corneum.[5] Sprayable emulsions with high filter concentrations have also been tested for skin penetration in vitro.[6]

Wikipedia notes primary research reporting minimal skin penetration and no estrogenic effect in an in vitro assay or a rat uterotrophic test.[2] Grokipedia reports low acute toxicity and no evidence of irritation in standard tests.[1]

Bisoctrizole has been measured in European North and Baltic Sea sediment in a hazard assessment,[7] tested on brine shrimp and microalgae,[8] and included in an eco-compatibility assessment of newer-generation sunscreens.[9]
It is permitted in the EU (Grokipedia cites up to 10%) and in Canada, Australia and Japan; it has not been approved by the US FDA.[1][2]

In the United States, sunscreens are regulated as over-the-counter drugs and not as cosmetics, which Wikipedia describes as the reason that fewer filters are available there than in many other countries [11]. The 2014 Sunscreen Innovation Act aimed to speed approval of new filters, but the pace did not change immediately [11]. In 2021 the FDA sorted existing filters into categories, and as of that year only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide were classed as generally recognised as safe and effective [11]. Wikipedia reports that a Time and Extent Application for bisoctrizole has been submitted to the FDA, while it is approved in the EU at up to 10% [11]. The same article lists 29 compounds approved in the EU and 17 in the US as of 2023, and says the FDA proposed bemotrizinol, a related Tinosorb-family filter, for approval in 2025 as the first new US sunscreen ingredient in 20 years [11].

A registered Phase 2 trial (n=16, 2007) evaluated microfine titanium dioxide, pigmentary titanium dioxide and bisoctrizole, alone and in combination, in people with idiopathic solar urticaria.[10] No other human trials specific to bisoctrizole were found; the in vivo UVA assessment of MBBT formulations is the other human-measured dataset.[4]

card.summary: A particle-form UV filter (Tinosorb M) that covers UVA and UVB; common abroad, not US-approved.
card.note: Not an FDA-approved sunscreen active; Wikipedia flags some property claims as weakly sourced.

quick.overview:
Bisoctrizole is a sunscreen ingredient sold as microfine particles. It absorbs UVA and UVB and is sometimes described as a hybrid between chemical and mineral filters.

It is approved in the EU and several other regions, but not by the US FDA.
quick.mechanism: The particles absorb UV and dissipate it as heat. It is often used alongside other filters.
quick.risks: Sources describe minimal skin penetration and no estrogenic activity in lab tests. Environmental studies have measured it in sediment and tested aquatic species.
